turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Mr Pillay. Pop your arm out, I'm just doing your blood pressure and pulse before the doctor calls you.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Is it going to pinch? These things always pinch. Are we late already, because the parking had me in a state.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): No needles from me. Blood pressure is one hundred and forty-eight over eighty-six, pulse seventy-two, oxygen sat ninety-seven percent. He'll be with you just now.
[SEG0004] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Thanks, sister. He's been twitchy since we left home.
[SEG0005] person_4 (DOCTOR): Howzit, I'm Doctor Naidoo. Ag, this computer is crawling, one second... right. What's brought you in?

[SEG0006] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm his wife. He's seventy-six. I live with him and I run the medicines. He'll say he's fine, but he asks the same questions over and over, he's been missing appointments, and last Tuesday he got lost driving back from Pick n Pay in Wynberg.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, no. I'm fine. I don't repeat myself. Why am I here, am I in some sort of trouble?
[SEG0008] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the screen jumped. Say that again, what's actually been going on?
[SEG0009] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He repeats himself. This morning he asked me four times which day the bins go out. It's been close on a year, since last winter, more or less.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): That's not... a year? No. I don't ask her twice. I'm not a child, doctor. Can we just go?
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hold on. The getting lost, tell me about that.

[SEG0012] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Last Tuesday, after Pick n Pay in Wynberg. He phoned me from the robot by the station and he couldn't tell if he should turn for Kenilworth. A petrol attendant had to point him. A ten-minute drive took nearly an hour.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I was not lost. I knew where I was. I took the long way round the roadworks, that's all. She fusses. Is this going to sit on my file for good?
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm not building a case, I'm listening. Any falls lately?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I haven't fallen. My legs are perfectly fine. Why, do you think I'm about to fall over?
[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): No falls. He holds the rail, but he hasn't gone down.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): And chest pain, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain, and I'm not short of breath. I walk to the gate every morning. Is it my heart, then?
[SEG0019] person_3 (CAREGIVER): While that thing thinks about it, did you see the Proteas last night? That catch at backward point, shame, I nearly spat my tea.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Ag, only the highlights on my phone. The rain delay in Centurion dragged on forever, they could have covered the pitch ages before.

[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): My grandson in Stellenbosch bowls left-arm spin for the under-thirteens. Phones me about his googly and his favourite fast bowler and nothing else. Twelve, and already taller than his mother.
[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): We meant to drive up for his match on Saturday, but the petrol price, so we stayed in and braaied. The wind had the serviettes in the neighbour's yard.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): Ja, the weather's been mad, boiling one day and that cold front off the sea the next. Anyway. I drifted, sorry.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. The appointments he missed, which were those?
[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The dentist, two weeks back, and the optometrist the month before. Both were on the calendar. He walked straight past them.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't forget appointments. The dentist I remembered. She's exaggerating, she always does this. Are you going to believe her over me?
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sorry, wrong tab again. Mrs Pillay, the appointments, once more, slowly.
[SEG0028] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Dentist two weeks ago, he never pitched. Eye test the month before, same thing. I found the cards in his jacket afterwards.

[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): All right. All right. The dentist, ja, I wrote Wednesday and it was the Tuesday, so I missed it. And I do ask her about the bins more than once. I hear myself and then I can't remember if I already asked. There. Are you satisfied?
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): That helps, thank you. Any headache, or weakness down one side?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No headache. No weakness. So it can't be a tumour if there's no headache, isn't that right? Please tell me it isn't a tumour.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm not putting a name on it today, Mr Pillay. I'm not guessing. We need bloods and a proper memory assessment before anyone says anything.

[SEG0033] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The tablets, since I do the pill box. Amlodipine in the morning for his blood pressure, five milligrams, and atorvastatin twenty milligrams at night for the cholesterol.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No, the blood pressure tablet is ten milligrams. I've been on ten for ages. Don't you let her change it. Are you changing my tablets today?

[SEG0035] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Joe, the box from the chemist says five milligrams. I've packed it like that for two years. Mind you, I have caught him at the cupboard, so I can't swear he only takes what's in the box.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): Say the doses again, please. I was typing in the wrong field.

[SEG0037] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Amlodipine, packet says five milligrams every morning, he insists it's ten. Atorvastatin twenty milligrams at night, no argument there. And I still can't be sure he isn't taking an extra some days.
[SEG0038] person_4 (DOCTOR): Bring the boxes next time and we'll settle the amlodipine. Any allergies, medicines or anything else?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. No allergies. Will the tests have dye? I'm useless with needles, is there a big needle?
[SEG0040] person_3 (CAREGIVER): No allergies that I know of, and I've known him forty years.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me listen a moment. Heart sounds are normal, chest is clear, and there's no weakness in the arms or the legs.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): So I'm healthy? Then what's the fuss? How long is this memory test? Do they make you draw a clock? If I fail, do I lose my licence?

[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm not taking your licence today. I'd rather your wife does the driving until the assessment's done, just to be safe. It's a chat and some paper tasks, not a school exam.
[SEG0044] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He keeps the car keys in his pocket anyway. I'll drive.

[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): So. I'll send you for bloods: full blood count, kidney function, thyroid, vitamin B12 and a glucose. And I'll book a memory assessment at the clinic. No label from me until those are back.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Bloods for what, is it cancer? Do I get the results the same day? Can she come into the memory test? What if they say I can't live at home anymore?
[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): The bloods are to look for things we can actually treat, not to hunt for cancer. Not same-day results. She can come with you. Nobody is talking about moving you out.
[SEG0048] person_1 (NURSE): Lab downstairs can take the bloods today, or tomorrow morning if you'd rather. I'll leave the form at reception just now.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Tomorrow, before breakfast? For how many hours, and am I allowed water? I don't want to feel awful in the queue.

[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): Nothing to eat from about ten the night before if you come in the morning. Water is fine. Come back and see me in three weeks. The bloods should be through, and we might have a date from the memory clinic.
[SEG0051] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Three weeks. I'll put it in my phone, not on his calendar. Thanks, doctor.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): And if I get lost again before that, what do I do, do I phone you? Is there a number on the card? I'm not trying to be difficult, I just need to know.
[SEG0053] person_4 (DOCTOR): If you get properly lost, or something new crops up, phone the rooms and we'll fit you in sooner. Otherwise I'll see you in three weeks. Try not to stew on it.
